content: For HIV-negative children and adolescents, monitoring should occur at 2 weeks and 4 weeks after starting treatment, at the end of the intensive phase (2 months), and then every 2 months until treatment completion (4 or 6 months, depending on the regimen). For those living with HIV, monitoring should occur at 2 weeks, 4 weeks, and then monthly until treatment completion. Children with advanced HIV should be monitored more frequently, following existing guidelines for advanced HIV care. Caregivers of children and adolescents on TB treatment should receive education about the disease, medications, dosages, preparation, and potential side effects. It is essential to confirm that caregivers understand this information and are aware of how to manage side effects if they occur. Caregivers should also be shown how to use and update treatment cards, which should be reviewed at each visit to discuss adherence and side effects. Additionally, the need for transportation or nutritional support should be assessed and provided if available. Treatment outcomes are determined at the end of the treatment period, which is 4 months for shorter regimens and 6 months for standard regimens. Monitoring should include assessing the resolution or persistence of TB symptoms, side effects of medications, weight gain (to adjust dosages as needed), and adherence to the treatment regimen. Sputum samples for smear microscopy may be collected at 2 months and at treatment completion for children who were bacteriologically positive at diagnosis, provided the treatment site has the capacity to perform these tests. However, symptomatic improvement and weight gain are more reliable indicators of treatment success. Routine follow-up chest X-rays (CXR) are not necessary if the child is responding well to treatment, as radiographic abnormalities may persist even after successful treatment. Children who cannot produce sputum do not require repeat specimens at the end of treatment if the 2-month specimen is negative. Scheduled clinical monitoring after treatment completion is not required unless symptoms recur, in which case patients should return to the clinic for evaluation. If treatment is interrupted, the management depends on the phase of treatment and the duration of the interruption. For interruptions of less than 14 days during the intensive phase, treatment can continue, ensuring all doses are completed. Interruptions of 14 days or more require restarting the intensive phase. In the continuation phase, the approach depends on the percentage of doses completed and the cumulative duration of the interruption. If less than 80% of doses are completed and the interruption exceeds 1 month (for 4-month regimens) or 2 months (for 6-month regimens), treatment should be restarted from the beginning of the intensive phase. If TB symptoms recur during an interruption, reassessment with molecular testing and drug susceptibility testing (DST) is necessary to evaluate for drug resistance. Treatment failure is defined as the need to terminate or change the treatment regimen due to lack of clinical or bacteriological response, adverse drug reactions, or evidence of drug resistance. Poor adherence is a common cause of treatment failure, and the possibility of multidrug-resistant (MDR) or rifampicin-resistant (RR) TB should be carefully assessed. Children with treatment failure should be evaluated for correct dosages, adherence, gastrointestinal absorption issues, medication toxicity, and other factors such as malnutrition or HIV-related complications. Children and adolescents requiring retreatment for TB should undergo rapid molecular testing to assess for drug resistance, particularly rifampicin and isoniazid resistance. Retreatment regimens should be informed by DST results. If resistance is detected, MDR/RR-TB regimens should be prescribed according to WHO recommendations. The reasons for treatment interruption, such as medication stockouts or adverse effects, should be addressed to prevent recurrence. All children diagnosed with TB should be registered with the National TB Program (NTP), regardless of the healthcare setting where they were diagnosed. Children diagnosed in hospitals who die before treatment initiation should also be registered. Growth monitoring and weight should be recorded at each visit to adjust dosages and assess treatment response. For children with MDR/RR-TB, treatment should be initiated promptly, even if bacteriological confirmation is pending. WHO recommends prioritizing shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimens for eligible patients. For those not eligible, individualized longer regimens should be constructed using medications from priority groupings. Bedaquiline and delamanid are now recommended for use in children of all ages, enabling the construction of all-oral regimens. Injectable agents, such as aminoglycosides, are no longer recommended due to their association with hearing loss and other adverse effects. In summary, the management of TB in children and adolescents requires careful monitoring, adherence support, and individualized treatment plans based on drug susceptibility profiles. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment are critical to improving outcomes and reducing mortality.
